catalog_quote: This process of vowel reduction is undoubtedly an effect of phonetic stress. In a protoform with two syllables, only the one receiving stress was preserved, while the unstressed vowel eventually disappeared (e.g., *ˈmate > mat). ... this resulted in vowel-final lexemes that systematically received primary stress on their penultimate syllable, and secondary stress every second syllable leftward (e.g., *ˌsaŋaˈpulu). Vowel reduction affected word-medial as well as word-final posttonic syllables, which explains why words with four syllables were regularly reduced to two: for example, *ˌsaŋaˈpulu > MSN saŋˈwul. The loss of word-final posttonic vowels explains why, in essentially all the languages of the area, words are now systematically stressed on their final rather than their penultimate syllable (contra Lynch 2000:77). new_statements.rule_in_words: In the modern Torres-Banks languages, Lemerig among them, word stress falls on the final syllable: the Proto-Oceanic penultimate-stressed vowel became the last surviving vowel once post-tonic vowels were lost (*máte > mat), so the historically stressed syllable is now word-final.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Stated only for the proto-stage: 'secondary stress every second syllable leftward' from the penult (trochaic, right-aligned). Nothing said about secondary stress in modern Lemerig.
new_statements.exceptions: The rule is hedged as holding in 'essentially all the languages of the area'; the exceptions are not named. Mota is the evident exception (it kept final vowels, *mate > mate, sec. 3.2 p. 451). Lemerig lost all post-tonic vowels (Table 4 p. 476: 'loss of posttonic V2? all'), so the final-stress outcome applies to it.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress ('words are now systematically stressed'), stated areally for the 17-language corpus in a historical-phonology article, not as a Lemerig-specific synchronic description; no discussion of citation forms, phrase stress, or the prosody of prefixed article + noun (except the 2007 remark that the article carries no primary stress).
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog leme1238 = ISO 639-3 [lrz] Lemerig, created 2009 by ISO change request 2008-069 (François) splitting the former [vlr] 'Vatrata' into Vera'a [vra] and Lemerig [lrz]. The Ethnologue 'dialects' Leon, Pak (Bek/Päk) and Sasar are earlier varieties of Lemerig; Codrington 1885's 'Pak' and 'Leon and Sasar' sketches therefore describe Lemerig varieties (and are silent on accent). François's modern data (2-3 last speakers, Päk variety mainly) underlie all the statements quoted here; the 2005 stress statement is areal (17 Torres-Banks languages), not specific to Lemerig.

readall_conflicts: No source opened here says anything about Lemerig stress, so there is no direct conflict on Lemerig. Indirectly: Lynch 2000 pp. 59 and 77 (following Crowley's TOL sketch) describes the neighbouring Banks language Mwotlap as having regular penultimate-syllable stress (ˈnɛ-vɛt 'stone', ˈna-tmʷan 'man', ˈkɛmɛm 'we'), whereas François 2005:451 (the catalog's source for Lemerig) states 'contra Lynch 2000:77' that in essentially all languages of the area words are stressed on the final syllable after loss of post-tonic vowels, and François's own Mwotlap grammar (2001, held under motl1237) gives systematic final stress for Mwotlap. That disagreement is about Mwotlap and the area, resolved by the primary fieldworker in favour of final stress; it does not alter the Lemerig record.

sources.note: Sec. 3.1 p. 451: proto-forms had penultimate primary stress and secondary stress every second syllable leftward; after loss of word-final post-tonic vowels 'in essentially all the languages of the area, words are now systematically stressed on their final rather than their penultimate syllable (contra Lynch 2000:77)'. Lemerig (LMG) is one of the 17 languages (Table 1 p. 445) and lost all post-tonic vowels (Table 4 p. 476), so falls under the rule; no Lemerig-specific synchronic stress statement.
